questions.question: When does Spring call a method annotated with `@PostConstruct`?
options: Before the constructor, so the object can prepare its fields
Once, after the object is created and its dependencies are injected
Every time another bean calls a method on this bean
Only when the application context is being closed
questions.explanation: `@PostConstruct` belongs to the initialization phase: Spring first instantiates the object (constructor), injects dependencies, runs Aware callbacks, and then calls the method once so it can, for example, fill a cache. Running at context close is what `@PreDestroy` does.

questions.question: A bean implements `BeanNameAware`. What does its `setBeanName(String name)` method represent?
options: A callback in which Spring gives the bean the name it is registered under
A method the bean must call to register itself with the container
A setter you can call from `main` to rename the bean inside the container
A method that runs only when the bean is destroyed
questions.explanation: Aware interfaces are callbacks where information flows from the container to the bean, which is why the method is a setter. If you call `setBeanName("userBean2")` yourself, as in the lecture's commented code, it is just an ordinary method call and does not change the name registered in the container.

questions.question: In a plain Spring 7 project that only depends on `spring-context` (no Spring Boot), `import jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct;` does not compile. What is the fix used in the lecture?
options: Change the import to `javax.annotation.PostConstruct`, which is built into the JDK
Replace `@PostConstruct` with `@Bean` on the method
Add the `jakarta.annotation:jakarta.annotation-api` dependency to `pom.xml`
Upgrade `spring-context` to a Spring Boot starter version
questions.explanation: Spring 6/7 uses the `jakarta.annotation` package, and without Spring Boot you may need to add `jakarta.annotation-api` yourself, exactly as the lecture's `pom.xml` does (version 3.0.0). The old `javax.annotation` classes are not part of modern JDKs and are not what Spring 6+ expects; `@Bean` registers beans, it is not an init callback.

questions.question: A singleton bean is marked `@Lazy` and nothing eager depends on it. What happens to it during container startup?
options: It is instantiated, but dependency injection and `@PostConstruct` wait until first use
It is fully created and initialized, but its `@PreDestroy` is disabled
Nothing at all - Spring does not even read its bean definition until it is requested
Only its BeanDefinition is registered; instantiation, injection and initialization all happen when it is first requested
questions.explanation: For a lazy singleton, Spring reads and registers the bean definition at startup but delays the whole object journey - creation, dependency injection, Aware and init callbacks - until someone asks for the bean. Spring must know the definition up front, otherwise it could not create it on demand.

questions.explanation: The documented order is `@PostConstruct`, then `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()`, then the custom `initMethod`. All of them run during startup because the bean is an eager singleton, so "ready" comes last. In real projects you would pick just one mechanism.

questions.question: A singleton `PaymentService` has a `@PreDestroy` method that prints "Cleaning up". `main` does `ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);`, uses the bean and returns, but "Cleaning up" never appears. What is the fix?
options: Make the bean prototype, because only prototypes get destruction callbacks
Use a `ConfigurableApplicationContext` (or `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext`) reference and call `context.close()` (or register a shutdown hook)
Move the cleanup code into the constructor
Call `System.gc()` so the garbage collector triggers `@PreDestroy`
questions.explanation: Destruction callbacks run when the container shuts down, and in a plain (non-web) Spring program nothing closes it unless you do. The `ApplicationContext` interface has no `close()`, which is why the lecture declares `ConfigurableApplicationContext` and calls `context.close()`. Garbage collection is unrelated to Spring's callbacks, and prototypes are the beans that do NOT get destroyed.

questions.question: Why is `@PostConstruct` or a custom `initMethod` usually preferred over implementing `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()`?
options: Because `afterPropertiesSet()` runs before dependencies are injected
Because `InitializingBean` only works for prototype beans
Because `afterPropertiesSet()` is called on every method invocation
Because implementing `InitializingBean` ties the class to a Spring-specific interface
questions.explanation: All three run after dependency injection, but `InitializingBean` forces the class to implement a Spring interface, coupling business code to the framework. `@PostConstruct` is a standard Jakarta annotation, and `initMethod` keeps the class a plain object. `afterPropertiesSet()` runs once, for any scope.

questions.explanation: On `getBean` the prototype goes through constructor -> Aware callbacks (bean name, then context) -> `@PostConstruct`, which fills the map, so `getValue(1)` is "Aditya". Spring hands prototype instances to the caller and does not track them, so `context.close()` does not call `@PreDestroy` on it. The default bean name of `CartService` is `cartService`.

questions.question: A prototype bean `PaymentSession` opens a network connection in `@PostConstruct` and closes it in `@PreDestroy`. In production you see connections leaking even though the app calls `context.close()` on shutdown. Why, and what should you do?
options: Spring does not track prototype instances after handing them out, so `@PreDestroy` is not called; the caller must release the resource itself (e.g. explicit close / try-with-resources)
`@PreDestroy` only runs if the bean also implements `DisposableBean`; implement it as well
`context.close()` only destroys lazy beans; remove `@Lazy` from the configuration
The garbage collector runs `@PreDestroy` later, so the leak is temporary and needs no fix
questions.explanation: For prototypes Spring manages the beginning of the lifecycle (create, inject, initialize) but not the end; keeping references to every instance would itself leak memory. So destruction callbacks are not called, and expensive resources must be released by the code using the object. Garbage collection never invokes Spring's destruction callbacks.

questions.question: The lecture breaks an A <-> B dependency with `@PostConstruct`. Both classes are scanned components in package `in.strikes`, and `Main` is in the same package. What happens?
options: Startup fails with a circular-dependency exception
It prints `true`
It prints `false`, because B received a different A instance
A `NullPointerException` in `setB()`, because `b` is not injected yet when `@PostConstruct` runs
questions.explanation: Only A needs B at construction time; B has a no-arg constructor, so Spring creates B, then A with B injected. `@PostConstruct` runs after injection, so `b` is set and `b.setA(this)` hands B the very A singleton the container holds - `true`. There is no constructor cycle, so nothing fails.
